dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A clinic offers genetic testing that can predict a baby's risk of a serious inherited disorder before birth. Some families welcome it; others worry about what happens when we start choosing which lives are 'worth' having.
dilemma.prompt: Where should the line be drawn on using this technology?

options.text: Offer it freely — information empowers families
options.outcome: This choice maximizes autonomy and can prevent suffering, but risks quietly pressuring families toward 'acceptable' children.

options.text: Allow it only for serious disorders
options.outcome: This tries to balance prevention with ethics, but someone must define 'serious' — and that definition will always be contested.

options.text: Restrict it heavily until society agrees on rules
options.outcome: This protects against misuse but delays help for families who could act on it now.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Scientists can now edit genes in crops to make them drought-resistant — feeding more people on less water. Critics worry about unknown long-term effects on ecosystems and who owns the seeds.
dilemma.prompt: Should India bet big on gene-edited crops?

options.text: Yes — climate change won't wait for perfect certainty
options.outcome: This bets on scientific evidence and urgent need; the risk is accepting unknowns that only time reveals.

options.text: Yes, but with public seed ownership
options.outcome: This accepts the science while protecting farmers from corporate control — harder to fund, fairer to share.

options.text: No — protect existing ecosystems first
options.outcome: This chooses caution, but caution has a cost: farmers facing failed monsoons don't get the option of certainty either.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A state with a linguistic minority must decide how to run its schools and government offices. The majority says one language unifies; the minority says it erases them.
dilemma.prompt: What does power-sharing actually demand here?

options.text: One official language for efficiency
options.outcome: Administratively simple — but 'unity by uniformity' is exactly what power-sharing exists to prevent.

options.text: Two languages with equal status
options.outcome: Costlier and slower, but the minority's dignity is protected — the whole point of sharing power.

options.text: Local language locally, majority language for state functions
options.outcome: A federal-style compromise — works only if 'local functions' aren't quietly made second-class.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A political party can win an election by appealing to one religion's voters, or take the harder road of building a coalition across communities. The first path is faster. The second is harder.
dilemma.prompt: Is winning by division ever justified if the party then governs well?

options.text: Yes — good governance redeems a divisive campaign
options.outcome: This judges ends over means — but the campaign's damage to social trust doesn't vanish when the government performs.

options.text: No — the method poisons the outcome
options.outcome: This holds that democracy's rules matter as much as results — a government built on division carries that division into power.

options.text: It depends on how deep the division goes
options.outcome: The realist's answer — but 'acceptable' division is a line everyone draws differently, and moving it is how democracies erode.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A country develops fast under a strong central government that limits criticism. A slower, messier democracy next door protects dissent but delivers less growth.
dilemma.prompt: Which country would you rather live in — and what does 'outcome' even mean?

options.text: The fast one — growth is the outcome that matters
options.outcome: Defensible — until the criticism you'd want to make becomes illegal to voice.

options.text: The democratic one — the process IS the outcome
options.outcome: Democracy's defenders argue the ability to change course peacefully is worth more than any single result.

options.text: Neither is pure — judge by who's protected
options.outcome: The most honest lens: ask not 'how fast did it grow' but 'what happened to the people who disagreed'.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A district can raise its average income by attracting one large factory, or spread the same money across hundreds of small farms. The average looks identical. The lives don't.
dilemma.prompt: Is 'development' the average or the distribution?

options.text: The factory — big growth lifts everyone eventually
options.outcome: The growth-first argument; 'eventually' is the word every displaced farmer learns to distrust.

options.text: The farms — development that isn't shared isn't development
options.outcome: The distribution argument; slower numbers, but the money reaches people who need it now.

options.text: Both — but in the right order
options.outcome: The sequencing answer — which is really saying: who bears the cost during the transition matters most.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A multinational brings jobs to an Indian town but pays less than it would abroad and ships profits home. A local company pays fairly but can't compete on price and is closing.
dilemma.prompt: Is globalisation good when it saves jobs but squeezes them?

options.text: Take the jobs — some income beats none
options.outcome: True for the worker today; the question is whether 'today' becomes a permanent arrangement.

options.text: Protect the local company
options.outcome: Keeps value and dignity local, but protection can hide inefficiency until the protection itself fails.

options.text: Take the jobs AND fight for better terms
options.outcome: The hard middle — requires worker organizing and regulation, which is exactly what globalisation pressures governments to skip.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A forest houses both a tiger reserve and villages that have grazed cattle there for generations. Conservationists want the villages moved; the villagers say the forest was theirs before it was a reserve.
dilemma.prompt: Whose forest is it?

options.text: The tigers' — ecosystems can't vote
options.outcome: Protects a species that has no other voice; the cost falls entirely on people who can least afford it.

options.text: The villagers' — they conserved it first
options.outcome: Honors generational stewardship; but grazing pressure on a shrinking forest is real, whoever owns it.

options.text: Both — make villagers paid guardians
options.outcome: The model some reserves actually use — turns the conflict into employment, but only if the payments are real and permanent.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A dam will irrigate 200 villages downstream but submerge 30 upstream. The math is clear; the homes are not.
dilemma.prompt: How should the decision be made?

options.text: Build it — 200 villages outweigh 30
options.outcome: The utilitarian answer; it treats 'villages' as interchangeable units and ignores that the 30 lose everything while the 200 gain somewhat.

options.text: Don't build — displacement is a wrong no benefit erases
options.outcome: The rights-first answer; principled, but the 200 downstream villages' water shortage is also a harm, just a quieter one.

options.text: Build only if the displaced get a real share
options.outcome: The just-compensation answer — land for land, a stake in the dam's benefits — rarely offered fully, which is why this question keeps returning.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: During the freedom movement, some Indians chose non-violent resistance; others believed the empire only understood force. Both loved the same country.
dilemma.prompt: Was violence ever the right answer to colonialism?

options.text: Non-violence won — anything else would've lost legitimacy
options.outcome: Gandhi's bet: moral force made the empire's violence visible. It worked — but slowly, and many died waiting.

options.text: Force was justified against a violent empire
options.outcome: The revolutionary argument — occupation is itself violence; refusing to answer it can read as acceptance.

options.text: The question is wrong — the movement needed both
options.outcome: Historians note the non-violent mainstream and revolutionary fringe each made the other's position stronger.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Nuclear power offers enormous clean energy — and waste that stays dangerous for millennia, plus the rare catastrophic failure. Solar is safer but can't yet power a steel plant at night.
dilemma.prompt: Should nuclear be part of India's energy future?

options.text: Yes — coal kills more people than nuclear ever has
options.outcome: Statistically true — air pollution's toll dwarfs reactor accidents; but statistics don't calm a community near a plant.

options.text: No — don't make waste that outlives your grandchildren
options.outcome: The intergenerational ethics argument; but refusing nuclear often means accepting fossil fuels, which harm grandchildren too.

options.text: Yes, with storage solved BEFORE scaling
options.outcome: The engineering-honesty answer — build the waste solution first; the risk is 'later' never arriving.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Prenatal screening can detect chromosomal disorders early. Families get information to prepare — or to make choices. The same technology that helps some families grieve prepares others to never begin.
dilemma.prompt: Does knowing early help or harm?

options.text: It helps — preparation is love
options.outcome: For many families it is — knowing early changes outcomes. The technology itself is neutral; the choice it enables is not.

options.text: It harms when 'screening' becomes 'selecting'
options.outcome: The disability-rights worry: screening normalizes the idea that some lives shouldn't start. Both things can be true.

options.text: It depends entirely on the counselling around it
options.outcome: Most genetic counsellors' actual position — the test is a tool; the conversation around it decides whether it's care or eugenics.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A village can develop faster if young people leave for city jobs and send money home — or slower if they stay and build local work. Both paths help the village; neither helps it the same way.
dilemma.prompt: Is migration progress or a slow emptying?

options.text: Progress — remittances fund what the village can't
options.outcome: Remittances genuinely build schools and houses; the cost is paid in missing sons and daughters.

options.text: Emptying — the village loses its builders
options.outcome: Also true — the people who could create local opportunity are precisely the ones who leave.

options.text: The real failure is making them choose
options.outcome: Rural development's actual goal: a village where staying is a real option, not a sacrifice.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Reproductive-health education reduces disease and unsafe practices, but some communities worry it conflicts with their values or rushes children into adult topics.
dilemma.prompt: Should schools teach it regardless?

options.text: Yes — health literacy is a right, not a preference
options.outcome: Public health's position — information withheld is a harm; but taught without cultural care, it can alienate the families who need it most.

options.text: Yes, but shaped with community input
options.outcome: The pragmatic middle — content stays accurate, delivery respects context; slower, but it actually reaches people.

options.text: No — families should decide the timing
options.outcome: Respects family authority; the risk is that the students who most need the information are exactly those whose families don't provide it.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: The same electromagnetic physics that powers MRI machines also powers missile guidance. A physics graduate can build either.
dilemma.prompt: Does the scientist share responsibility for the use?

options.text: No — knowledge is neutral, choices belong to users
options.outcome: The purist position; historically incomplete — the physicists who built the first atomic bomb disagreed with it afterward.

options.text: Yes — you can't un-know what your work enables
options.outcome: The responsibility position; but almost no physics is use-specific — the same math does both.

options.text: Share responsibility for foreseeable misuse
options.outcome: Most ethics codes' actual answer — you're accountable for what you could reasonably predict, not for every possible use.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Plastics transformed medicine, food safety and daily life — and are now in the oceans, the food chain, and human blood. Banning them helps the environment; it also raises costs for the poorest.
dilemma.prompt: Can a material be both a miracle and a mistake?

options.text: Ban single-use first — keep it where it matters
options.outcome: The surgical approach — plastic in hospitals, not in grocery bags; requires alternatives to actually exist affordably.

options.text: Ban broadly — half-measures haven't worked
options.outcome: The urgency argument; honest that bans without substitutes shift cost to those least able to pay.

options.text: Fix recycling instead of banning
options.outcome: Technically appealing — but decades of 'recyclable' plastic have mostly not been recycled; the honest question is whether this time is different.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A family can send a bright child to coaching for a competitive exam — expensive, but the exam opens doors — or to a good local college near home. The exam path risks everything on one test.
dilemma.prompt: Is investing in one child at the cost of stability ever justified?

options.text: Yes — human capital is the family's real wealth
options.outcome: The investment argument; it works only if the child succeeds — and the family's risk if they don't is real.

options.text: No — security first, ambition within means
options.outcome: The prudent path; but 'within means' can quietly cap what a bright child from a poor family is allowed to attempt.

options.text: Invest — but never make the child carry the whole family's hope
options.outcome: The emotionally honest answer — the financial bet may be right; the weight placed on one teenager is the part to refuse.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A state government wants to build a highway its people need; the central government controls the funds and wants conditions attached. Both are elected; both claim to represent the people.
dilemma.prompt: When state and centre disagree, whose mandate wins?

options.text: The state's — they know their people's needs
options.outcome: Federalism's core logic — proximity to the problem; but national projects cross borders by definition.

options.text: The centre's — national interest outranks regional
options.outcome: The unity argument; taken too far it hollows out the states federalism was designed to protect.

options.text: Neither — negotiation IS the federal system working
options.outcome: The textbook answer that's also true — friction between levels isn't a bug; it's the check working.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: An economy can grow fast by extracting resources now, or sustainably by growing slower. The fast path shows results this decade; the sustainable path pays off for the next generation.
dilemma.prompt: Who is growth actually for?

options.text: Now — poverty today can't wait for tomorrow's environment
options.outcome: The urgency argument; the trap is that 'now' never ends — there's always another urgent reason to postpone sustainability.

options.text: Tomorrow — growth that destroys its own foundation isn't growth
options.outcome: The sustainability argument; the honest cost is slower improvement for people living now.

options.text: Both — the only wrong answer is pretending there's no trade-off
options.outcome: Development economics' real position — green growth is possible but costs more upfront; someone has to fund that difference.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Industrialisation brought factories, jobs and progress — and child labour, poisoned rivers, and workers losing their craft. It was both a miracle and a disaster, in the same decade.
dilemma.prompt: Was industrialisation progress?

options.text: Yes — the long-run gains outweigh the short-run pain
options.outcome: True in aggregate; but 'short-run pain' was whole lifetimes — a worker crushed in 1850 didn't see the long run.

options.text: Yes, but the pain was a choice, not a necessity
options.outcome: The sharper answer — industrialisation could have come with protections; it chose speed over workers.

options.text: Progress is a question for each person it touched
options.outcome: The honest answer — progress measured in GDP looks different than progress measured in a weaver's hands.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Hydrogen fuel promises clean energy — but most hydrogen today is made from natural gas, and 'green' hydrogen needs enormous renewable electricity that could power homes directly.
dilemma.prompt: Is hydrogen the future or a detour?

options.text: The future — hard-to-electrify sectors need it
options.outcome: True for steel, shipping, fertiliser — where batteries can't reach; the risk is spending scarce renewables on hydrogen where direct electrification works.

options.text: A detour — electrify what you can first
options.outcome: The efficiency argument — every electron into green hydrogen loses ~30% of its work; but some sectors have no electric path at all.

options.text: Both — the honest question is WHERE hydrogen goes
options.outcome: The engineering answer — hydrogen for what can't electrify, wires for what can; the fight is about which is which.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A stem-cell treatment could repair damaged tissue — but the research uses cells whose origins some communities object to. The science works; the ethics of how it got here are contested.
dilemma.prompt: Should a treatment be judged by its source or its result?

options.text: The result — healing is the highest value
options.outcome: The compassionate argument; it sidesteps that how research happens shapes what research becomes acceptable.

options.text: The source — some means corrupt any end
options.outcome: The deontological position; it protects research ethics but tells a patient the principle outweighs their recovery.

options.text: Both — and 'alternatives exist' changes the answer
options.outcome: The practical resolution — when another path exists, prefer it; when none does, the question gets harder honestly.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Chemical fertilisers and pesticides tripled India's harvest — and are now linked to soil decline and farmer debt. A farmer choosing organic feeds fewer people but farms sustainably.
dilemma.prompt: Can a farmer afford to farm the 'right' way?

options.text: Go organic — soil is the real capital
options.outcome: Right for the long term; the farmer eating this year faces yields that drop before they recover.

options.text: Keep chemicals — yields first, fix soil later
options.outcome: The survival argument; 'later' has been postponed for fifty years and the soil keeps score.

options.text: Transition with support — don't ask farmers to pay for the change alone
options.outcome: The policy answer — subsidies for the transition period; the question is whether policy arrives before the soil runs out.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: An algorithm decides who gets a loan, a job interview, a scholarship. It's faster and cheaper than human review — and it learned from biased data nobody fully audited.
dilemma.prompt: Is an unfair algorithm better than an unfair human?

options.text: Yes — it applies its bias consistently
options.outcome: Consistency is something — but a consistently wrong system is wrong at scale, on every applicant, every time.

options.text: No — at least a human can be argued with
options.outcome: The appeal argument — you can persuade a person; an algorithm's 'no' has no one home to hear the objection.

options.text: Neither — audit it like you'd audit a human process
options.outcome: The engineering-ethics answer — transparency, bias testing, appeal paths; possible, but only if someone requires it.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Laws of motion let us design safer cars — crumple zones that sacrifice the car to save the passenger. A cheap car without them costs half as much; a family choosing it may be choosing between money and physics.
dilemma.prompt: Should safety features be mandatory even if they raise prices?

options.text: Yes — physics doesn't care about your budget
options.outcome: The regulation argument — momentum at 60 km/h is non-negotiable; but mandates price out the families who could only afford the cheap car.

options.text: No — let buyers choose their trade-off
options.outcome: The autonomy argument; it assumes buyers fully understand the physics of what they're declining.

options.text: Mandate the minimum, subsidise the rest
options.outcome: The design answer — a safety floor for everyone, help for those who can't reach it.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A moneylender charges desperate farmers 5% a month. A bank won't lend to them — no collateral. Banning the moneylender removes the only credit available; allowing him keeps the debt trap running.
dilemma.prompt: Is bad credit better than no credit?

options.text: Yes — survival needs money today, not policy
options.outcome: True in the emergency; but 'bad credit available' is how the debt trap stays permanent.

options.text: No — the trap is worse than the drought
options.outcome: Protects the long term; a farmer facing a failed crop this month may not get a long term.

options.text: Neither — the answer is making formal credit reach them
options.outcome: The structural fix — SHGs and microcredit exist precisely because both options fail alone.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A genetically modified mosquito could collapse a malaria-carrying population. Release it and a disease that kills children could shrink. Release it and you can't call it back.
dilemma.prompt: Is irreversible prevention better than preventable deaths?

options.text: Release it — children are dying now
options.outcome: The urgent-compassion answer; the risk is ecological effects that only appear years after the decision.

options.text: Wait — 'can't be recalled' demands certainty
options.outcome: The precautionary answer; each year of waiting is a year of deaths that certainty didn't prevent.

options.text: Release it in stages — contained first, wild only after data
options.outcome: The staged answer — slower, but 'irreversible' isn't a reason to skip the reversible steps.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A party can field a candidate with a criminal record who wins reliably, or a clean candidate who might lose. The seat decides who controls the government.
dilemma.prompt: Does a 'necessary' win excuse a compromised candidate?

options.text: Yes — losing means no chance to do good at all
options.outcome: The realist argument; every party that says this keeps the pipeline of compromised candidates full.

options.text: No — the means define what you'd do with power
options.outcome: The integrity argument — a party that wins by compromising candidates has already shown what it will do in office.

options.text: The voters should know and decide
options.outcome: Transparency as the minimum — but information alone hasn't stopped criminal-record candidates from winning.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: The 1991 reforms opened India's economy — growth accelerated, inequality widened, and whole sectors of protected industry collapsed. Thirty years later, both results are still visible.
dilemma.prompt: Were the reforms worth it?

options.text: Yes — the alternative was stagnation
options.outcome: Largely supported by growth data; the cost is measured in the industries and communities that didn't survive the transition.

options.text: Yes, but the safety net should have come first
options.outcome: The critique most economists accept now — reform without protection for the displaced made the cost unnecessarily brutal.

options.text: Mixed — worth asking the workers who lost, not just the economy that grew
options.outcome: The distributional answer — the aggregate won; the question is whether 'the economy' includes the people it ran over.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Groundwater lets farmers grow water-hungry crops in dry regions — a lifeline that's emptying aquifers faster than rain refills them. Today's harvest borrows from tomorrow's water.
dilemma.prompt: Should the government restrict what farmers pump?

options.text: Yes — an empty aquifer helps nobody
options.outcome: The sustainability answer; restrictions without alternatives punish farmers who have no other water source.

options.text: No — farmers' livelihoods aren't negotiable
options.outcome: The livelihood answer; but 'no restriction' is also a decision — to let the resource end.

options.text: Restrict new borewells, support the shift to dry crops
options.outcome: The transition answer — honest that some farmers will farm differently or not at all; the support decides whether that's fair or cruel.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: An accountant discovers the company's books hide a loss — correcting it means honesty, a falling stock price, and possibly layoffs; staying quiet keeps everyone employed a while longer.
dilemma.prompt: Is a kind lie still a lie?

options.text: Report it — books exist to be true, not kind
options.outcome: The professional-ethics answer; the layoffs that follow are real, and so is the trust the correction preserves.

options.text: Stay quiet — protecting jobs matters more than ledgers
options.outcome: The compassionate-looking answer; but hidden losses don't disappear — they compound, and the reckoning lands harder.

options.text: Report it AND fight for the workers the truth affects
options.outcome: The complete answer — honesty about the books, advocacy for the people; harder than either option alone.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Print culture spread ideas — and propaganda. The same press that carried reform movements carried hate pamphlets. Every technology of free speech is also a technology of its abuse.
dilemma.prompt: Is a freer press always better?

options.text: Yes — the answer to bad speech is more speech
options.outcome: The liberal tradition's answer; it assumes good ideas win, which history only sometimes confirms.

options.text: Yes, but platforms shape what wins
options.outcome: The structural answer — 'free' doesn't mean flat; the press's owners and algorithms decide which speech travels.

options.text: Freedom without literacy is a weapon, not a right
options.outcome: The education answer — print's danger was never print; it was readers who couldn't tell pamphlet from paper.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Bacteria evolve antibiotic resistance because we overuse antibiotics — in medicine AND in farm animals raised for meat. Stopping farm use helps everyone's future; it raises food prices now.
dilemma.prompt: Who pays for antibiotic stewardship?

options.text: Ban farm use — resistance is a shared emergency
options.outcome: The public-health answer; the cost lands on farmers and on the price of food — someone absorbs it either way.

options.text: Regulate, don't ban — target misuse not use
options.outcome: The surgical answer — treatment stays, growth-promotion goes; only works if enforcement is real.

options.text: Let the market decide — consumers pay for antibiotic-free
options.outcome: The market answer; the poorest consumers can't pay the premium, so the cheapest meat keeps the practice alive.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A talented student-athlete can pursue professional sport — a short, uncertain career with a narrow peak — or a safer academic path that closes the sporting door.
dilemma.prompt: How should a young person weigh a dream against odds?

options.text: Take the shot — peak windows don't reopen
options.outcome: The dream argument — true, and honest only if there's a plan for the 99% who don't make it.

options.text: Take the safer path — the dream can be a hobby
options.outcome: The prudent argument; a sport pursued as a hobby is not the same as one pursued as a life.

options.text: Both for a defined window — set a real deadline
options.outcome: The bounded-bet answer — pursue the dream seriously until a chosen date, with a real fallback built, not imagined.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A mining region's economy runs on coal — jobs, power, the town's whole life. The coal must eventually end; the question is whether the town ends with it.
dilemma.prompt: How does a place survive the end of its reason to exist?

options.text: Mine until it's gone — don't kill the town early
options.outcome: The survival answer; 'until it's gone' guarantees the town dies with no preparation at all.

options.text: Transition now — painful but survivable
options.outcome: The just-transition answer — works only if the 'just' is funded; retraining programs have a poor record without it.

options.text: Mine smarter AND build what comes next in parallel
options.outcome: The parallel-track answer — the town doesn't stop living while it changes; it requires believing in a future it can't yet see.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A welfare program gives cash directly — dignity and freedom of choice — or gives goods/services — guaranteed nutrition and housing but no autonomy. Cash respects; goods protect.
dilemma.prompt: Is help more respectful when it trusts, or when it guarantees?

options.text: Cash — people know their own needs best
options.outcome: The dignity argument — evidence mostly supports it; the failure cases are the ones that make headlines.

options.text: Goods — protection beats autonomy when hunger's the risk
options.outcome: The safety argument; honest that it treats the recipient as someone who can't be trusted with their own welfare.

options.text: Cash by default, goods where markets fail
options.outcome: The design answer — autonomy where shops exist, goods where they don't; the hard part is knowing which is which.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A community's traditions give it identity — and include practices that harm some members (early marriage, exclusion of certain groups). Respecting culture and protecting individuals pull in opposite directions.
dilemma.prompt: When does 'respect for culture' become an excuse?

options.text: Protect the individual — rights outrank tradition
options.outcome: The rights-first answer; imposed from outside it can destroy the very community fabric that also protects people.

options.text: Respect the culture — change must come from within
options.outcome: The internal-reform answer; slower, but the people inside the practice are the ones it happens to.

options.text: Support the insiders already fighting for change
options.outcome: The solidarity answer — the community's own reformers know both the tradition and the harm; they need backing, not replacement.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Probability powers insurance — a pool where everyone pays a little so nobody loses everything. The same math powers gambling apps — engineered to make the house win while feeling fair.
dilemma.prompt: Is the math responsible for how it's used?

options.text: No — probability is a tool, not an intent
options.outcome: True of the math itself; the app designer's intent is a different question the math doesn't answer.

options.text: Yes — understanding it means seeing the exploitation
options.outcome: The literacy answer — whoever can compute expected value can see the game is rigged; teaching the math is itself a defense.

options.text: Regulate the use, not the math
options.outcome: The policy answer — probability stays free; gambling apps get odds-disclosure requirements most users never read.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: CRISPR can edit a human embryo to remove a deadly disease — the edit is permanent and passes to every descendant. The same technique could someday select height, eye colour, maybe intelligence.
dilemma.prompt: Is preventing disease worth opening the door to designing humans?

options.text: Yes — a child free of disease justifies the risk
options.outcome: The compassionate answer; 'the door' isn't hypothetical — every precedent makes the next edit easier to justify.

options.text: No — germline edits are forever
options.outcome: The precautionary answer — mistakes propagate; but refusing also means watching children born with preventable suffering.

options.text: Yes for disease only — a hard legal line at enhancement
options.outcome: The boundary answer — draw the line where suffering ends and preference begins; the hard part is that line moves.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A consumer can buy the cheap product made in poor conditions, or the expensive fair one. Buying fair costs more; buying cheap keeps the cheap system running.
dilemma.prompt: Is a consumer's wallet a vote?

options.text: Yes — every purchase is a choice about what continues
options.outcome: The ethical-consumption answer; true but incomplete — the cheapest option isn't a 'choice' for people who can't afford another.

options.text: No — the system decides what's on the shelf
options.outcome: The structural answer — individual choices can't reach what was never offered; regulation reaches further than wallets.

options.text: A vote if you can afford to cast it
options.outcome: The honest answer — consumer power is real but unequally distributed; the wallet-vote works best when it's not the only mechanism.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Nomadic peoples built mobile civilizations across the steppe — and their raiding destroyed settled communities. History remembers them as both empire-builders and destroyers.
dilemma.prompt: How should we judge peoples whose survival depended on others' loss?

options.text: Judge by their time — survival had different rules
options.outcome: The historical-context answer; honest about the era, but it risks excusing what the people being raided experienced as pure catastrophe.

options.text: Judge by the harm — context doesn't erase victims
options.outcome: The victim-centred answer; but applied alone it flattens history into a ledger of blame.

options.text: Hold both — understand without absolving
options.outcome: The historian's actual craft — explain why it happened AND name what it cost; the two jobs don't cancel.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Understanding the nervous system lets us build better prosthetics and brain-computer interfaces — and raises the question of who owns the neural data a device records.
dilemma.prompt: Should your brain's data have special protection?

options.text: Yes — neural data is the last private frontier
options.outcome: The privacy-maximalist answer; the risk is regulation that slows devices that could restore movement to the paralyzed.

options.text: No — data is data, protect it like everything else
options.outcome: The uniform-privacy answer; it underestimates that neural data reveals intent, not just behaviour.

options.text: Yes — but only for data that reveals thought, not function
options.outcome: The surgical answer — protect what the device infers, not what it measures; the hard part is telling them apart.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A city's cameras catch real criminals — and record everyone else, always. The footage solved a murder last month; it also logs who visited which clinic, which protest, which door.
dilemma.prompt: Is safety worth being always watched?

options.text: Yes — the innocent have nothing to hide
options.outcome: The common argument; 'nothing to hide' assumes the watcher will always be benign — history doesn't.

options.text: No — a watched population is a managed one
options.outcome: The civil-liberties answer; it asks citizens to accept risks the watched never chose.

options.text: Only with deletion clocks and independent audits
options.outcome: The governed-surveillance answer — the camera can stay if the footage expires and someone outside the system checks it.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Natural hazards — floods, earthquakes — become disasters mainly where poverty forced people into dangerous places. The hazard is natural; the vulnerability is built.
dilemma.prompt: Is a 'natural' disaster ever really natural?

options.text: The hazard is natural — the disaster is political
options.outcome: The framing disaster-research actually uses — nature provides the event; human choices provide the casualties.

options.text: Both are natural — people have always lived in risky places
options.outcome: Historically true; but 'always lived there' often meant 'had nowhere else to go'.

options.text: Doesn't matter — prepare either way
options.outcome: The pragmatist answer; but preparation designed for the wrong cause protects the wrong things.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A textile factory pollutes a river its workers' families drink from. Closing it poisons nobody; it also pays nobody. Regulating it costs money that may move the factory elsewhere.
dilemma.prompt: Whose job is it to make the factory clean?

options.text: The factory's — pollution is a cost of doing business
options.outcome: The polluter-pays principle; the factory can also simply leave, taking the jobs and keeping the practice elsewhere.

options.text: The government's — public health is a public duty
options.outcome: The regulatory answer; only works where the regulator is stronger than the industry it regulates.

options.text: Shared — cleaner tech funded jointly, jobs kept
options.outcome: The cooperative answer; requires the factory to stay, which means the clean-up must be cheaper than leaving.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Infrastructure projects — roads, ports — unlock growth but displace communities and cost ecosystems. Every development decision is also a decision about who bears the cost.
dilemma.prompt: Can development be both fast and fair?

options.text: Fast — delays are their own injustice
options.outcome: The urgency answer; 'fast' has a history of meaning 'fast for some, displaced for others'.

options.text: Fair — speed that breaks people isn't development
options.outcome: The process answer; slower, and honest that some urgent needs genuinely can't wait.

options.text: Fast where consent is real, slow where it isn't
options.outcome: The consent-calibrated answer — the pace should match whether the people affected actually agreed.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A pharmaceutical company prices a life-saving drug high to recover research costs — research that made the drug possible. Generics could make it affordable but cut the profit that funds the next drug.
dilemma.prompt: Who's right — the patient or the pipeline?

options.text: The patient — a drug nobody can afford saves nobody
options.outcome: Access-first reasoning; the counterweight is that without profit, the next drug may never exist.

options.text: The pipeline — today's price funds tomorrow's cure
options.outcome: The innovation argument; honest about economics, cold about who dies waiting for tomorrow.

options.text: Both — public funding for research, open access for medicine
options.outcome: The structural answer — pays the pipeline with taxes instead of patients; requires public willingness to fund it.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A government wants sweeping powers to fight a security threat — surveillance, faster trials, fewer checks. Supporters say safety demands it; critics say safety that costs liberty isn't safety.
dilemma.prompt: How much freedom should safety cost?

options.text: Some — rights without security are theoretical
options.outcome: True — but 'temporary' powers have a habit of becoming permanent; every democracy that's lost them started this way.

options.text: None — rights are the point of the country
options.outcome: The principled position; absolute versions of it have struggled when the threat is real and immediate.

options.text: Only with a sunset — powers that expire and must be re-argued
options.outcome: The constitutional answer — emergency powers that auto-expire force each generation to re-justify them.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A town can build a road through a wetland — cutting commute times for thousands — or around it, costing more and taking longer. The wetland doesn't get a vote.
dilemma.prompt: How do you weigh what can't speak for itself?

options.text: Build through — people's time is the priority
options.outcome: The direct-benefit answer; wetlands' value is real but invisible until the floods come.

options.text: Build around — some costs aren't on the invoice
options.outcome: The long-view answer; costs more now, protects flood-buffering and habitat nobody priced.

options.text: Build through but fund wetland restoration elsewhere
options.outcome: The mitigation answer — honest that the original wetland is still lost; offsets work only if actually delivered.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A company can cut costs by automating — or keep jobs it doesn't strictly need. Shareholders want efficiency; the town needs the jobs.
dilemma.prompt: Does a company owe its workers more than the market requires?

options.text: No — efficiency is what lets companies survive
options.outcome: The market argument — a company that keeps unnecessary jobs may fail entirely, losing all of them.

options.text: Yes — a company is also a community member
options.outcome: The stakeholder argument — businesses that benefit from a town owe it something beyond the legal minimum.

options.text: It owes transition, not stasis
options.outcome: The modern answer — automate, but fund retraining; the job may not be saved, the worker should be.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A mountain region needs a hydropower dam for electricity and a growing economy — but the mountains are geologically young, landslide-prone, and home to communities who live downstream of the proposed site.
dilemma.prompt: How much risk is acceptable for power?

options.text: Build with the best engineering available
options.outcome: The development answer — risk managed, not zero; the communities downstream carry the remainder.

options.text: Don't build in fragile geology — find power another way
options.outcome: The precautionary answer; power has to come from somewhere, and the alternatives have their own costs.

options.text: Build only if the people downstream decide, not just the ones who benefit
options.outcome: The consent answer — risk-bearers should have the vote, not just the benefit-receivers.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: An entrepreneur can make a product cheaper using a supplier with poor labour practices — winning on price — or a fair supplier whose higher costs may sink the business before it starts.
dilemma.prompt: Does 'just starting out' excuse the cheap choice?

options.text: Yes — survive first, fix ethics at scale
options.outcome: The survival argument; but 'later' rarely arrives — the supply chain you start with tends to be the one you keep.

options.text: No — ethics aren't a premium feature
options.outcome: The integrity argument; risks the business never existing to be ethical at all.

options.text: Choose fair AND compete on something besides price
options.outcome: The differentiation answer — 'ethically made' is itself a market; harder, but it makes the choice sustainable.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Gravitational physics made GPS possible — free to everyone, precise to metres. The same physics guides weapons to the same precision. Einstein's equations are on both sides.
dilemma.prompt: Can a scientist choose which uses their work enables?

options.text: No — fundamental knowledge belongs to everyone
options.outcome: The openness argument; the counter is that 'everyone' includes the ones you'd least want to enable.

options.text: Yes — publish selectively, patent defensively
options.outcome: The controlled-release answer; it works for applied work but fails for the fundamentals — physics can't be unpublished.

options.text: You choose the field, not the use — pick fields carefully
options.outcome: The career-ethics answer — a physicist chooses what to work on; the uses that follow are harder to control but not unknowable.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: E-waste recycling recovers gold and copper — done formally, safely; done informally, by workers who burn circuit boards and breathe the fumes because it's the only job available.
dilemma.prompt: Is informal recycling livelihood or poisoning?

options.text: Ban it — the fumes are a public-health emergency
options.outcome: The health answer; a ban without alternative income turns a poisoning into a starvation.

options.text: Formalize it — train and equip the same workers
options.outcome: The just-transition answer — keeps the livelihood, removes the poison; requires someone to fund the equipment.

options.text: Regulate the producers — make electronics makers pay for safe recycling
options.outcome: The extended-responsibility answer — the cost lands where the product was made; only works where enforcement reaches.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A writer must choose between writing in English — reaching a global audience, earning more — or in their mother tongue — preserving a language, reaching a smaller home audience.
dilemma.prompt: Does reach justify abandoning your own language?

options.text: Write in English — ideas matter more than the vessel
options.outcome: The reach argument; every writer who chooses this makes the home language's literature a little thinner.

options.text: Write in the mother tongue — a language dies by desertion
options.outcome: The preservation argument; the smaller audience is real, and so is what only that language can say.

options.text: Write in both — translate yourself
options.outcome: The dual answer — doubles the work, keeps both doors open; the rarest choice because it's the hardest.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Food preservatives and additives keep food safe and affordable for millions — and the same chemistry enables ultra-processed foods linked to poor health.
dilemma.prompt: Is 'safe chemistry' still safe when it makes unhealthy food possible?

options.text: Yes — preservation prevents real harm (spoilage, hunger)
options.outcome: The food-safety answer — additives prevented deaths before they enabled junk food; the technology isn't the problem, the use is.

options.text: No — 'safe' compounds in an unhealthy system aren't safe
options.outcome: The systems answer — a preservative that's individually harmless still serves a food system that's collectively harmful.

options.text: The chemistry is neutral — regulate the food system it serves
options.outcome: The regulatory answer — additives pass safety tests; the question is what products they're allowed to make cheap.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A democratically elected government can legally pass a law that a minority community experiences as unjust. Everything was done by the rules; the outcome still harms.
dilemma.prompt: Is a law legitimate just because it was democratically passed?

options.text: Yes — process is what makes law law
options.outcome: The procedural answer; but 'legally passed' has sheltered every unjust law that ever existed.

options.text: No — rights exist above majority votes
options.outcome: The constitutional answer — democracies have courts precisely for this; the check only works if it's allowed to work.

options.text: Legitimate procedurally, contestable morally
options.outcome: The complete answer — the law is legal AND can still be wrong; democracy's test is whether the wrong can be challenged.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Agricultural biotechnology can grow more food on less land with less water — and concentrates seed ownership in a few companies who control what farmers plant.
dilemma.prompt: Is feeding more people worth concentrating control of food?

options.text: Yes — hunger is the emergency, ownership is secondary
options.outcome: The food-security answer; true until the concentrated ownership itself creates the next emergency.

options.text: No — who controls seeds controls everything after
options.outcome: The sovereignty answer; refusing the technology has costs too — yields that don't rise as populations do.

options.text: Yes with public seeds — the tech in public hands
options.outcome: The structural answer — public-sector breeding keeps the yield without the lock; requires funding public research adequately.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: A vaccine exists for a disease that mainly kills in poor countries. Developing it cost billions; the countries that need it can least afford it.
dilemma.prompt: Should medicine be priced by what it cost or by who needs it?

options.text: By cost — unfunded research doesn't happen
options.outcome: The innovation answer; honest that it means the poorest wait longest for the medicine they need most.

options.text: By need — a medicine that doesn't reach the sick failed
options.outcome: The access answer; without the pipeline of profitable drugs, the next vaccine never gets funded.

options.text: Tier it — rich countries pay full price, poor ones pay cost
options.outcome: The differential-pricing answer — actually used for HIV drugs; works only if wealthier markets accept subsidizing the rest.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Regional parties give voice to local identities — and can fragment national policy into a hundred vetoes. Unity needs a centre; identity needs a voice.
dilemma.prompt: Is federalism strength or friction?

options.text: Strength — a nation that can hold its differences is stronger than one that hides them
options.outcome: The pluralist answer; the friction is the price of not forcing sameness.

options.text: Friction — a hundred vetoes can stall what everyone needs
options.outcome: The efficiency answer; true in the short term, and the short term is where political careers are measured.

options.text: Both — the friction IS the system checking itself
options.outcome: The constitutional-design answer — federalism wasn't designed to be fast; it was designed to be hard to capture.

dilemma.title: A real-world call
dilemma.scenario: Light-based technologies — lasers, surgery, communications — heal and connect; they also enable precision weapons and surveillance systems.
dilemma.prompt: Should scientists refuse work with dual uses?

options.text: Yes — know your work's worst use before you do it
options.outcome: The conscientious answer; but almost no field is single-use — refusal mainly removes conscientious people from the work.

options.text: No — you can't control applications from the lab
options.outcome: The purist answer; honest about the limits of control, silent about the choice of what to work on.

options.text: Choose the field, publish openly, fight misuse in the open
options.outcome: The engaged answer — the scientist's real leverage is in what they choose to pursue and what they say about its use.
